newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - Analysts cool on Nordic telecoms merger talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts cool on Nordic telecoms merger talk.

text.p: Talk of a merger between Nordic telecoms majors LM Ericsson Ab and Nokia Oy lent seasonal spice to their shares amid a broad rally in tech stocks, but few analysts' mouths were watering on Thursday.

Shares in both companies rose again in early trade after advancing sharply both in Europe and Wall Street on Wednesday as brokers cited merger rumours from London, but by midsession were already falling back as analysts found the idea ill-informed.
"I think it's nothing to do with Nokia and Ericsson merging -- the European Union would shoot that down in 10 minutes," said Neil Barton at Merrill Lynch in London.
Combined, the Swedish and Finnish firms would virtually control mobile infrastructure markets in Italy, Spain, Britain and the Nordic markets, said Richard Kramer at Goldman Sachs.

"There's been such a strong rally in tech stocks in the last few months -- people want to present a good portfolio to imply they've had a part in this and give their owners a warm feeling," said Barton.

The Standard & Poor's Technology Index, which started advancing sharply at end-July after a wobbly start to the year, on December 10 hit a new life-high of 596.57, and blue chip tech stocks surged in New York on Wednesday amid broad demand.
Analysts noted that with stock markets recently vulnerable to sharp mood swings, other tech share prices have spurted ahead on scant fundamentals and with volume quite thin.

Beyond the monopoly question, they saw scant benefit in a merger: "They have a very different architecture of products and very different cultures inside the companies," said Kramer. "Knowing the technology ... there's a lot of overlap and not many areas where they could borrow from one another."

The two are keen rivals -- Ericsson outranks Nokia in terms of the size of its infrastructure business and Nokia is bigger than Ericsson in mobile handset sales -- but both are beefing up their respective relative weaknesses, analysts said.

Neither company would comment on the rumours, but Nokia spokesman Seppo Harkkonen said the two currently collaborate very little -- essentially only in working towards technology standards and membership of international associations.
In the past they investigated working together on SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) technology, but that did not work out, Kramer said.
"These are the two most innovative companies in mobile," said Barton. "They need each other as creative competitors."

A Finnish analyst, who declined to be named, said Nokia's status as Finland's flagship high-tech company is of such vital importance here -- economically, politically and emotionally -- that even an attempted merger would probably fail.
"Even if Nokia is a global company, the heart of Nokia is Finnish," she said. "Would the Nokia engineers who work all hours do the same thing for Ericsson? I doubt it."

By 1145 GMT Ericsson, which advanced nine crowns in Stockholm on Wednesday, was off 0.5 crowns at 205.5. Nokia, which added nine markka at the Helsinki open to 264.00 markka, trimmed gains to 260.50, up 5.50.
